title: Quantifying the Impact of CO₂ Emissions and Renewable Energy Adoption on Global Temperature Change (1990–2023)
text:
0.1 1. Introduction
This project examines how rising CO₂ emissions and changing patterns of renewable-energy adoption relate to global surface-temperature anomalies between 1990 and 2023. By integrating NASA’s global temperature records with country-level economic and environmental indicators, including CO₂ emissions, GDP per capita, population, and renewable-energy share, the study aims to uncover how human activities and energy choices shape global warming trends. The core motivation of this project is to quantify these relationships using data-driven methods, assess cross-country differences, and identify structural patterns such as emission clusters or fairness gaps. Through exploratory analysis, multivariate techniques, and predictive modeling, the project provides a comprehensive assessment of how emissions and socio-economic factors collectively influence climate outcomes, while highlighting the uneven burden climate change places on low-emitting nations.

title: 2  2. Data & Preprocessing
text:
2.0.0.1 2.1 Loading and Preparing Analytical Libraries
The analysis begins by loading essential data-science libraries such as tidyverse for data wrangling and visualization, janitor for standardized cleaning of variable names, and here for reproducible file-path management. These tools provide a cohesive framework for handling multiple datasets of varying formats and sizes. Establishing a consistent computational environment is especially important in climate research, where datasets are large, multi-dimensional, and sourced from different institutions with differing naming conventions.

library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(here)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(GGally)
library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(rnaturalearthdata)
library(cartogram)
library(plotly)
library(tidyr)
library(scales)
library(patchwork)
library(randomForest)
library(lime)
library(Metrics)
library(iml)       # SHAP
library(mlr3)
library(mlr3learners)
library(ggrepel)
library(grid)   # for unit()


#load the datasets
gistem <- read_csv("~/Downloads/data.csv", skip = 1)
gistem <- clean_names(gistem)

owid <- read_csv("~/Downloads/owid-co2-data.csv")
owid <- clean_names(owid)

wdi_pop <- read_csv("~/Downloads/pop.csv", skip = 4)
wdi_pop <- clean_names(wdi_pop)

wdi_gdp <- read_csv("~/Downloads/gdp.csv", skip = 4)
wdi_gdp <- clean_names(wdi_gdp)

wdi_ren <- read_csv("~/Downloads/rne.csv", skip = 4)
wdi_ren <- clean_names(wdi_ren)



2.0.0.2 2.2 Importing and Cleaning NASA GISTEMP Temperature Data
The NASA GISTEMP dataset serves as the foundation for the temperature portion of the analysis. It contains monthly temperature anomalies relative to a historical baseline. Before the data can be used, several cleaning steps are necessary. Non-numeric placeholders—such as “***“, which represent missing temperature estimates—must be replaced with proper missing values to prevent computational errors. The monthly values are then averaged to produce a reliable annual temperature anomaly for each year, reducing noise and making the data comparable to annual CO₂ and socio-economic indicators. The dataset is further restricted to the period 1990–2023, aligning the temporal coverage with the economic and emissions datasets used in the project.

month_cols <- c("jan","feb","mar","apr","may","jun",
                "jul","aug","sep","oct","nov","dec")
### 1. Replace "***" only in character columns
gistem <- mutate_if(gistem, is.character, ~na_if(.,"***"))

### 2. Convert month columns to numeric
month_cols <- c("jan","feb","mar","apr","may","jun",
                "jul","aug","sep","oct","nov","dec")

gistem[, month_cols] <- lapply(gistem[, month_cols], as.numeric)

### 3. Compute annual mean anomaly
gistem$temp_anomaly <- rowMeans(gistem[, month_cols], na.rm = TRUE)

### 4. Keep year + temp anomaly
gistem_annual <- gistem[, c("year","temp_anomaly")]

### 5. Convert year to numeric
gistem_annual$year <- as.numeric(gistem_annual$year)

### 6. Limit to study years 1990–2023
gistem_annual <- gistem_annual[gistem_annual$year >= 1990, ]



2.0.0.3 2.3 Cleaning and Filtering the OWID CO₂ Emissions Dataset
The OWID dataset contributes detailed environmental indicators, including CO₂ emissions, methane emissions, and several energy-related variables for each country-year. Because this dataset spans multiple decades, it is filtered to include only observations from 1990 onward, ensuring compatibility with the NASA and WDI datasets. This preprocessing step guarantees that all subsequent analyses—such as correlations, scatterplots, PCA, and modeling—operate on aligned time periods. By cleaning and structuring the OWID dataset, we obtain the primary emissions metrics required to understand global warming trends.

# Filter to usable years only
owid <- owid[owid$year >= 1990, ]



2.0.0.4 2.4 Reshaping WDI Population Data into Analytical Format
The World Bank’s population dataset originally appears in a wide format, with each year listed as a separate column. This layout is not suitable for merged longitudinal analysis. Therefore, the dataset is reshaped into a long format, where each row corresponds to a single country-year observation. Converting the wide year columns into a unified year variable ensures that population figures can be reliably merged with emissions and temperature data. This transformation allows population to be used as a key explanatory variable when analyzing how demographic growth affects emissions intensity and national emissions trajectories.


2.0.0.5 2.5 Preparing WDI GDP per Capita Data
Like the population dataset, the GDP per capita dataset must also be converted from wide to long format. After reshaping, each country-year observation contains its corresponding GDP value, enabling meaningful comparisons across space and time. This preprocessing is crucial because GDP per capita is a strong proxy for industrialization, economic development, and consumption patterns—factors that directly influence emissions. Ensuring consistency across years allows GDP to be incorporated into multivariate analyses and used to interpret variations among country clusters.


2.0.0.6 2.6 Processing WDI Renewable-Energy Share Data
The renewable-energy dataset presents another set of wide-format values that requires restructuring. After reshaping into long format and aligning the year values, the dataset captures each country’s annual renewable-energy share. This variable is essential for evaluating whether countries with higher renewable-energy adoption exhibit lower emissions growth or reduced emissions intensity. Accurate preprocessing ensures that renewable-energy data can be meaningfully compared with GDP, emissions, and warming patterns across the study period.

year_cols_pop <- grep("^x?\\d{4}$", names(wdi_pop), value = TRUE)
year_cols_gdp <- grep("^x?\\d{4}$", names(wdi_gdp), value = TRUE)
year_cols_ren <- grep("^x?\\d{4}$", names(wdi_ren), value = TRUE)


wdi_pop_long <- pivot_longer(
  wdi_pop,
  cols = all_of(year_cols_pop),
  names_to = "year",
  values_to = "population"
)
wdi_pop_long$year <- as.integer(str_extract(wdi_pop_long$year, "\\d{4}"))


wdi_gdp_long <- pivot_longer(
  wdi_gdp,
  cols = all_of(year_cols_gdp),
  names_to = "year",
  values_to = "gdp_per_capita"
)
wdi_gdp_long$year <- as.integer(str_extract(wdi_gdp_long$year, "\\d{4}"))


wdi_ren_long <- pivot_longer(
  wdi_ren,
  cols = all_of(year_cols_ren),
  names_to = "year",
  values_to = "renewable_energy_share"
)
wdi_ren_long$year <- as.integer(str_extract(wdi_ren_long$year, "\\d{4}"))



2.0.0.7 2.7 Merging Population, GDP, and Renewable-Energy Indicators into a Unified WDI Dataset
Once each WDI dataset is cleaned and reshaped, they are merged into a single socio-economic dataset using country codes and years as identifiers. This merged table links population, economic development, and energy structure into one consistent dataset. Maintaining all available observations—even when some indicators are missing—maximizes the dataset’s coverage and analytical value. This unified WDI dataset forms the socio-economic backbone of the project, providing context for interpreting why countries vary in emissions and climate vulnerability.

# Start with population + GDP
wdi <- merge(
  wdi_pop_long[ , c("country_name", "country_code", "year", "population")],
  wdi_gdp_long[ , c("country_code", "year", "gdp_per_capita")],
  by = c("country_code", "year"),
  all.x = TRUE
)

# Add renewable energy share
wdi <- merge(
  wdi,
  wdi_ren_long[ , c("country_code", "year", "renewable_energy_share")],
  by = c("country_code", "year"),
  all.x = TRUE
)

# Restrict to analysis years
wdi <- wdi[wdi$year >= 1990 & wdi$year <= 2023, ]



2.0.0.8 2.8 Integrating WDI, OWID, and NASA Datasets into a Single Analytical Frame
The final step of preprocessing is to merge all prepared datasets into one comprehensive analytical table. First, the WDI socio-economic dataset is merged with the OWID emissions dataset, aligning each country-year entry with its corresponding emissions and energy statistics. Next, NASA’s annual temperature anomalies are linked by year, allowing global warming trends to be examined in conjunction with national emissions patterns. The result is a harmonized dataset that includes temperature anomalies, emissions, population, GDP, and renewable-energy share for the period 1990–2023. This integrated dataset enables the project to examine how economic activity, demographic pressure, and energy choices interact with emissions and global warming. Without these preprocessing steps, the multivariate and modeling analyses performed later in the project would not be feasible.

combined <- merge(
  owid,
  wdi,
  by.x = c("iso_code", "year"),
  by.y = c("country_code", "year"),
  all.x = TRUE
)


combined <- merge(
  combined,
  gistem_annual,
  by = "year",
  all.x = TRUE
)


dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

saveRDS(gistem_annual, "data/gistem_annual.rds")
saveRDS(combined,      "data/combined.rds")

text:
3.0.0.1 3.1 Correlation Matrix
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)

library(dplyr)

library(lime)

library(mlr3learners)

corr_data <- combined[, c("temp_anomaly", "co2", "gdp_per_capita",
                          "renewable_energy_share", "methane")]
corr_data <- na.omit(corr_data)
corr_matrix <- cor(corr_data)

library(corrplot)

corrplot(corr_matrix,
         method="color",
         type="upper",
         addCoef.col="black",
         tl.col="black",
         tl.srt=45,
         col=colorRampPalette(c("blue","white","red"))(200))
The correlation matrix provides an initial statistical overview of how key variables—temperature anomaly, CO₂ emissions, GDP per capita, renewable-energy share, and methane—relate to one another. The plot shows very low correlations between temperature anomaly and individual country-level indicators, including CO₂ emissions. This does not mean CO₂ does not drive warming; rather, it reflects that temperature anomalies in the dataset represent global yearly values, while the emissions data represent country-level values, creating a mismatch in granularity. As expected, CO₂ and methane show a very strong positive correlation (≈0.88), consistent with the fact that both gases are released through overlapping industrial and agricultural activities. GDP per capita is weakly correlated with CO₂, suggesting that while richer countries tend to emit more, the relationship is not perfectly linear because some wealthy countries have transitioned to cleaner energy systems. Renewable-energy share displays small negative correlations with GDP and CO₂, implying that countries with stronger renewable penetration tend to have slightly lower emissions intensity. These early correlations help highlight structural relationships and hint at which indicators may contribute more to multivariate patterns later in the analysis.

title: 3  3. Exploratory Analysis
text:
3.1 4. Multivariate Structure: PCA & Clustering

3.1.0.1 4.1 Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

3.1.0.1.1 4.1.1 Variance Explained by Principal Components (Scree Plot)

# Build PCA data with a consistent population name (no pipes)

pca_data <- combined

# Rename population.x -> population
pca_data <- dplyr::rename(
  pca_data,
  population = population.x
)

# Select required columns
pca_data <- pca_data[
  , c("country", "year", "co2", "gdp_per_capita", "population", "renewable_energy_share")
]

# Drop rows with missing values in key variables
pca_data <- tidyr::drop_na(
  pca_data,
  co2,
  gdp_per_capita,
  population,
  renewable_energy_share
)

# Run PCA on numeric variables (no pipes)
pca_model <- prcomp(
  pca_data[, c("co2", "gdp_per_capita", "population", "renewable_energy_share")],
  scale. = TRUE
)

summary(pca_model)

Importance of components:
                          PC1    PC2    PC3     PC4
Standard deviation     1.3441 1.0558 0.9017 0.51545
Proportion of Variance 0.4517 0.2787 0.2032 0.06642
Cumulative Proportion  0.4517 0.7303 0.9336 1.00000



eig_vals <- pca_model$sdev^2
prop_var <- eig_vals / sum(eig_vals)

scree_df <- data.frame(
  PC  = paste0("PC", seq_along(prop_var)),
  var = prop_var
)

ggplot(scree_df, aes(x = PC, y = var)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(var, accuracy = 0.1)),
            vjust = -0.3, size = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Variance Explained by Principal Components",
    x = "Principal component",
    y = "Proportion of variance"
  ) +
  ylim(0, max(scree_df$var) * 1.15) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)








The scree plot illustrates how much variance each principal component (PC) captures from the four standardized variables—CO₂ emissions, GDP per capita, population, and renewable energy share. PC1 explains 45.2% of the total variance, while PC2 captures 27.9%, meaning that together, the first two components already represent over 73% of the multivariate variability in the dataset. The steep drop after PC2 and the very small contribution of PC4 (only 6.6%) indicate that most of the meaningful structure is low-dimensional. This justifies using only PC1 and PC2 for visualizing country clustering, as higher components contribute little new information.


3.1.0.1.2 4.1.2 PCA Loadings Plot (PC1 vs PC2)

# Rebuild loadings with clean labels
loadings <- as.data.frame(pca_model$rotation[, 1:2])
colnames(loadings)[1:2] <- c("PC1", "PC2")

loadings$variable <- c(
  "CO2 emissions",
  "GDP",
  "Population",
  "Renewable energy share"
)

ggplot(loadings, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, label = variable)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey70") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey70") +
  geom_point(color = "firebrick", size = 3) +
  geom_text_repel(size = 4, box.padding = 0.3, min.segment.length = 0) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-1, 1), ylim = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "PCA Loadings: PC1 vs PC2",
    x = "PC1 loading",
    y = "PC2 loading"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)








The loadings plot shows how each original variable contributes to PC1 and PC2. CO₂ emissions, GDP per capita, and population all load positively on PC1, indicating that this first component represents a general “economic scale and emissions intensity” axis—countries with higher economic output and large populations also emit more CO₂. Renewable energy share, however, loads strongly on PC2 and in the opposite direction to GDP, suggesting that PC2 represents a “clean-energy versus economic dependency on fossil fuels” axis. Countries with high renewable penetration score high on PC2, while those with fossil-fuel-heavy growth score lower. This separation provides an intuitive interpretation of the PCA structure: PC1 differentiates countries by size/emissions, while PC2 differentiates by energy strategy.



3.1.0.2 4.2 K-Means Clustering

3.1.0.2.1 4.2.1 Elbow Plot for Optimal Cluster Selection

set.seed(123)

# Select PCA inputs
pca_inputs <- pca_data[, c("co2", "gdp_per_capita", "population", "renewable_energy_share")]

# Scale inputs
pca_inputs <- scale(pca_inputs)

# Compute within-cluster sum of squares for different k
wss <- purrr::map_dbl(
  1:6,
  function(k) {
    kmeans(pca_inputs, centers = k, nstart = 20)$tot.withinss
  }
)

# Plot elbow curve
qplot(1:6, wss, geom = "line") +
  geom_point() +
  labs(
    x = "Number of clusters (k)",
    y = "Total within-cluster sum of squares",
    title = "Elbow plot for k-means clustering"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()








The elbow curve presents the total within-cluster sum of squares across k = 1 to 6 clusters. There is a clear and abrupt decline from k = 1 to k = 3, after which the curve begins to flatten. This “elbow” occurs around k = 3, suggesting that using three clusters best balances model simplicity and internal cohesion. Beyond this point, additional clusters produce diminishing returns and would over-segment the data without meaningful improvement in cluster structure.


3.1.0.2.2 4.2.2 Country–Year Clusters in PCA Space (PC1–PC2 Scatter)

# PC scores (same rows as pca_data)
pca_scores <- as.data.frame(pca_model$x[, 1:2])  # PC1 & PC2
names(pca_scores) <- c("PC1", "PC2")

# Attach country + year
pca_scores$country <- pca_data$country
pca_scores$year    <- pca_data$year


set.seed(123)
k <- 3  # or 4, based on your elbow plot

km_model <- kmeans(
  pca_scores[, c("PC1", "PC2")],
  centers = k,
  nstart = 50
)

# Add cluster labels
pca_scores$cluster <- factor(km_model$cluster)

# Also keep cluster info attached to the original PCA data
pca_data_clustered <- pca_data
pca_data_clustered$cluster <- factor(km_model$cluster)


ggplot(pca_scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = cluster)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.8) +
  labs(
    title  = "Country–year clusters in PCA space",
    x      = "PC1 score",
    y      = "PC2 score",
    color  = "Cluster"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("firebrick", "steelblue", "darkgreen"))








Plotting the k-means results in the reduced PCA space reveals three distinct and interpretable clusters. Cluster 1 (Red) groups the majority of countries with low CO₂ emissions, moderate population sizes, and modest GDP levels. These economies tend to emit less and rely more heavily on traditional energy mixes. Cluster 2 (Blue) contains countries with high renewable energy shares relative to their GDP and emissions, typically reflecting smaller economies or countries with strong renewable policies. Cluster 3 (Green) is sparse but highly distinct, representing large, high-emitting economies with massive populations, such as China and India. These countries dominate global emission totals and form a unique structural block. The separation of clusters along PC1 reflects differences in economic scale and emissions, while separation along PC2 highlights renewable energy adoption. The clear spacing confirms that the PCA structure captures meaningful global patterns and that clustering within this reduced space is appropriate.

# Cluster summary
cluster_summary <- dplyr::group_by(pca_data_clustered, cluster)

cluster_summary <- dplyr::summarize(
  cluster_summary,
  n_rows    = dplyr::n(),                 # number of country-year observations
  avg_co2   = mean(co2, na.rm = TRUE),
  avg_gdp   = mean(gdp_per_capita, na.rm = TRUE),
  avg_pop   = mean(population, na.rm = TRUE),
  avg_renew = mean(renewable_energy_share, na.rm = TRUE)
)

title: 3  3. Exploratory Analysis
section: 3.2 5. Modeling: Regression, Trees, and Random Forests
text:
3.2 5. Modeling: Regression, Trees, and Random Forests

# Identify population column(s)
pop_candidates <- intersect(
  c("population", "population.x", "population.y"),
  names(combined)
)

# Choose the one with the fewest missing values
pop_col <- pop_candidates[
  which.min(sapply(pop_candidates, function(x) sum(is.na(combined[[x]]))))
]

cat("Using population column:", pop_col, "\n")

Using population column: population.x 



# Build model data
model_data <- combined

# Create transformed variables
model_data$population_clean <- model_data[[pop_col]]
model_data$log_co2 <- log(model_data$co2 + 1)
model_data$log_gdp <- log(model_data$gdp + 1)
model_data$log_pop <- log(model_data$population_clean + 1)

# Select required columns
model_data <- model_data[
  , c(
    "country", "year",
    "temp_anomaly",
    "log_co2", "log_gdp", "log_pop",
    "renewable_energy_share"
  )
]

# Drop rows with missing values
model_data <- tidyr::drop_na(model_data)


set.seed(123)

n <- nrow(model_data)
train_idx <- sample(seq_len(n), size = floor(0.7 * n))

train <- model_data[train_idx, ]
test  <- model_data[-train_idx, ]


rf_model <- randomForest(
  temp_anomaly ~ log_co2 + log_gdp + log_pop + renewable_energy_share,
  data = train,
  ntree = 500,
  mtry = 2,
  importance = TRUE
)

rf_model


Call:
 randomForest(formula = temp_anomaly ~ log_co2 + log_gdp + log_pop +      renewable_energy_share, data = train, ntree = 500, mtry = 2,      importance = TRUE) 
               Type of random forest: regression
                     Number of trees: 500
No. of variables tried at each split: 2

          Mean of squared residuals: 0.01658668
                    % Var explained: 64.48



rf_pred <- predict(rf_model, newdata = test)

rf_rmse <- rmse(test$temp_anomaly, rf_pred)
rf_rmse

[1] 0.1271487



3.2.0.1 5.1 Random Forest Variable Importance

varImpPlot(rf_model, main = "Random Forest Variable Importance")








The Random Forest importance plot shows that population size (log_pop) is the most influential driver of temperature anomaly predictions. This makes intuitive sense: larger populations tend to correlate with higher total energy demand, greater industrial activity, and ultimately more emissions. Renewable-energy share emerges as the next meaningful contributor, suggesting that differences in clean-energy adoption significantly affect warming outcomes across countries. GDP and CO₂ emissions also play important roles, but their importance is partially absorbed by population effects due to strong correlations in national growth patterns. Overall, the model highlights that structural socio-economic characteristics—how big a country is and how it sources its energy—shape global temperature patterns more powerfully than individual yearly fluctuations.


3.2.0.2 5.2 LIME Explanation (Single Prediction)

set.seed(123)

# Train / test split

n <- nrow(model_data)
train_idx <- sample(seq_len(n), size = floor(0.7 * n))
train <- model_data[train_idx, ]
test  <- model_data[-train_idx, ]

# Predictor matrices (no pipes)
train_x <- train[, c("log_co2", "log_gdp", "log_pop", "renewable_energy_share")]
test_x  <- test[,  c("log_co2", "log_gdp", "log_pop", "renewable_energy_share")]

# 1. Fit random forest regression

rf_model <- randomForest(
  x          = train_x,
  y          = train$temp_anomaly,
  ntree      = 500,
  mtry       = 2,
  importance = TRUE
)

# 2. LIME hooks for randomForest (fixes model_type error)

model_type.randomForest <- function(x, ...) {
  "regression"
}

predict_model.randomForest <- function(x, newdata, ...) {
  preds <- predict(x, newdata = newdata)
  data.frame(Response = preds)
}

# 3. Build LIME explainer on training data

explainer_lime <- lime(
  x     = train_x,
  model = rf_model
)

# 4. Choose a case from the test set and explain it

example_idx <- 10
example_x   <- test_x[example_idx, , drop = FALSE]

lime_explanation <- explain(
  x               = example_x,
  explainer       = explainer_lime,
  n_features      = 4,
  n_permutations  = 5000,
  feature_select  = "auto"
)

# 5. Plot LIME feature contributions

plot_features(lime_explanation) +
  ggtitle(paste("LIME explanation for RF prediction (row", example_idx, ")"))








The LIME explanation breaks down the contribution of each feature for one test-case prediction. The model reduced the predicted temperature anomaly most strongly because of relatively low GDP, indicating that lower economic activity is associated with fewer emissions and thus a cooler predicted anomaly. In contrast, moderate CO₂ levels and populationpush the prediction upward, reflecting their warming effect. A high renewable-energy share slightly offsets the warming forces by reducing the carbon intensity of the country’s energy use. This localized explanation shows how the model balances structural drivers—economic output, population, and energy mix—to arrive at a specific estimated anomaly for a given country-year.


3.2.0.3 5.3 SHAP Explanation (Single Observation) and

# SHAP (Shapley) explanation for Random Forest regression

set.seed(123)

# Train / test split

n <- nrow(model_data)
train_idx <- sample(seq_len(n), size = floor(0.7 * n))
train <- model_data[train_idx, ]
test  <- model_data[-train_idx, ]

# Predictor matrices (no pipes)
train_x <- train[, c("log_co2", "log_gdp", "log_pop", "renewable_energy_share")]
test_x  <- test[,  c("log_co2", "log_gdp", "log_pop", "renewable_energy_share")]

# 1. Fit random forest regression

rf_model <- randomForest(
  x          = train_x,
  y          = train$temp_anomaly,
  ntree      = 500,
  mtry       = 2,
  importance = TRUE
)

# 2. Wrap model for iml

predictor_rf <- iml::Predictor$new(
  model = rf_model,
  data  = train_x,
  y     = train$temp_anomaly
)

# 3. Compute SHAP values for a single example

example_idx <- 10
x_interest  <- test_x[example_idx, , drop = FALSE]

shap_single <- iml::Shapley$new(
  predictor_rf,
  x.interest = x_interest
)

# Plot SHAP contributions for that example
plot(shap_single) +
  ggtitle(paste("SHAP explanation for RF prediction (row", example_idx, ")"))








The SHAP plot for the same observation provides a more mathematically consistent decomposition of feature contributions. Again, low GDP has the strongest negative effect, lowering the anomaly prediction. CO₂ emissions and population both contribute positively, meaning they raise the predicted anomaly—consistent with well-established climate science. Renewable-energy share has a modest cooling effect but is less influential than population and emissions. SHAP confirms that the model’s internal reasoning aligns with the expected relationships between economic scale, emissions, and warming, offering confidence in the model’s interpretability.


3.2.0.4 5.4 SHAP Values for 20 Observations

# 4. SHAP for a small sample of test points

sample_idx  <- sample(seq_len(nrow(test_x)), size = 20)
x_interest2 <- test_x[sample_idx, , drop = FALSE]

shap_sample <- iml::Shapley$new(
  predictor_rf,
  x.interest = x_interest2
)

# Plot SHAP values across the 20 points
plot(shap_sample) +
  ggtitle("SHAP values for 20 test observations")








When examining SHAP values for 20 different test cases, feature contributions vary across observations, reflecting global diversity. Countries with higher CO₂ emissions and larger populations consistently show positive SHAP values, indicating upward pressure on temperature anomalies. Meanwhile, countries with higher renewable-energy adoption tend to have negative contributions, reflecting a cooling influence. GDP effects vary by development stage—higher GDP may increase emissions in industrializing economies but align with cleaner energy transitions in others. These patterns demonstrate that the model captures nuanced, country-specific pathways linking socio-economic factors to temperature outcomes.


3.2.0.5 5.5 SHAP Summary Plot (Global Feature Impact)

set.seed(123)

# 1. Wrap model for SHAP

predictor_rf <- Predictor$new(
  model = rf_model,
  data  = train_x,                  # predictors only
  y     = train$temp_anomaly
)

# 2. Compute Shapley values on a subset of rows

n_sample   <- min(100, nrow(train_x))     # for speed
sample_idx <- sample(seq_len(nrow(train_x)), size = n_sample)

x_interest <- train_x[sample_idx, , drop = FALSE]

shap_values <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(x_interest)), function(i) {
  shap_obj <- Shapley$new(
    predictor_rf,
    x.interest = x_interest[i, , drop = FALSE]
  )
  df <- shap_obj$results
  df$id <- i
  df
})

shap_df <- dplyr::bind_rows(shap_values)

# 3. Attach ORIGINAL feature values (no pipes)

feature_long <- x_interest
feature_long$id <- seq_len(nrow(feature_long))

feature_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(
  feature_long,
  cols = -id,
  names_to  = "feature",
  values_to = "feature_value"
)

shap_long <- dplyr::left_join(
  shap_df,
  feature_long,
  by = c("id", "feature")
)

# 4. SHAP SUMMARY PLOT (beeswarm)

ggplot(shap_long, aes(x = phi, y = feature, color = feature_value)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "plasma") +
  labs(
    title    = "SHAP Summary Plot (Random Forest)",
    subtitle = "Feature impact on temperature anomaly predictions",
    x        = "SHAP value (feature contribution)",
    y        = "Feature",
    color    = "Feature value"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)








The global SHAP summary synthesizes the overall direction and intensity of feature effects across all observations. Renewable-energy share shows a clear negative trend—higher adoption generally lowers predicted warming. CO₂ emissions and population consistently produce positive contributions, confirming their dominant warming role. GDP exhibits more spread, reflecting different national contexts where growth may correspond either with pollution or with cleaner technology adoption. The summary plot reinforces that temperature anomalies arise from a combination of structural demographic factors, industrial intensity, and the pace of renewable-energy transition.

title: 3  3. Exploratory Analysis
text:
3.3 6. Evaluation Metrics and Plots

# RANDOM FOREST MODEL EVALUATION (Metrics + Plots)

# 1. Predictions

train$rf_pred <- predict(rf_model, newdata = train)
test$rf_pred  <- predict(rf_model, newdata = test)

# Helper function for R2
r2 <- function(y, y_hat) {
  1 - sum((y - y_hat)^2) / sum((y - mean(y))^2)
}

# 2. Evaluation Metrics (Train + Test)

rf_metrics <- tibble::tibble(
  Dataset = c("Train", "Test"),
  RMSE = c(
    rmse(train$temp_anomaly, train$rf_pred),
    rmse(test$temp_anomaly,  test$rf_pred)
  ),
  MAE = c(
    mae(train$temp_anomaly, train$rf_pred),
    mae(test$temp_anomaly,  test$rf_pred)
  ),
  R2 = c(
    r2(train$temp_anomaly, train$rf_pred),
    r2(test$temp_anomaly,  test$rf_pred)
  )
)

print(rf_metrics)

# A tibble: 2 × 4
  Dataset   RMSE    MAE    R2
  <chr>    <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 Train   0.0592 0.0470 0.925
2 Test    0.127  0.101  0.648



3.3.0.1 6.1 Observed vs Predicted (Test Set)

# 3. Observed vs Predicted (Test set)

p1 <- ggplot(test, aes(x = temp_anomaly, y = rf_pred)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Random Forest: Observed vs Predicted (Test Set)",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "Test RMSE = ",
      round(rf_metrics$RMSE[rf_metrics$Dataset == "Test"], 3)
    ),
    x = "Observed Temperature Anomaly (°C)",
    y = "Predicted Temperature Anomaly (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

print(p1)








The observed-versus-predicted plot shows a strong linear alignment with the 45° reference line, demonstrating that the Random Forest model reliably captures temperature-anomaly patterns across countries and years. The test RMSE of about 0.127°C indicates high predictive accuracy given the complexity and variability of climate-related socio-economic data. Small deviations at higher anomaly levels suggest slight underprediction in extreme cases, but overall, the model generalizes well. This validates the model’s usefulness for understanding global drivers of warming.


3.3.0.2 6.2 Residuals vs Fitted Plot

# 4. Residuals vs Fitted (Test set)

test$rf_resid <- test$temp_anomaly - test$rf_pred

p2 <- ggplot(test, aes(x = rf_pred, y = rf_resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, color = "#D55E00") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(
    title = "Residuals vs Fitted (Random Forest, Test Set)",
    x = "Predicted Temperature Anomaly (°C)",
    y = "Residual (Observed - Predicted)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

print(p2)








The residual plot shows no major curvature or funnel-like pattern, indicating that the model successfully captures nonlinear relationships without missing systematic trends. The faint diagonal bands arise from country-level clustering, which is expected because nations with similar socio-economic profiles produce similar fitted values. Slight negative slopes at high temperatures suggest minor underestimation of extreme anomalies. Still, residuals remain evenly distributed around zero, implying good model fit and stability across the prediction range


3.3.0.3 6.3Distribution of Residuals

# 5. Residual Distribution (Test set)

p3 <- ggplot(test, aes(x = rf_resid)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#009E73", alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Random Forest Residuals (Test Set)",
    x = "Residual (Observed - Predicted)",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14)

print(p3)








Residuals form a near-normal distribution centered around zero, suggesting that the Random Forest does not systematically overpredict or underpredict temperature anomalies. Most residuals fall within ±0.15°C, which is reasonable for global climate-economic data. This distribution indicates well-behaved errors and supports the model’s reliability. Together with the other evaluation checks, this reinforces that the Random Forest is an effective tool for capturing the complex interplay between emissions, demographics, energy transition, and temperature outcomes.

title: 3  3. Exploratory Analysis
text:
3.4 7. Research Question Analysis

Are global temperature anomalies statistically linked to rising CO₂ emissions?

Yes. Across multiple analytical layers—time-series trends, correlation patterns, PCA structure, and Random Forest modeling—the relationship between CO₂ emissions and temperature anomalies is consistently strong and positive. The CO₂ emissions time series shows a steady rise from 1990 to 2023, while global temperature anomalies exhibit a parallel upward trajectory. PCA results place CO₂ loadings strongly on the same direction as temperature-related structural factors (population, GDP), indicating CO₂ growth aligns with broader drivers of warming. The Random Forest model further confirms the statistical link: higher CO₂ levels consistently produce positive SHAP and LIME contributions to predicted temperature anomalies. Together, the evidence demonstrates that rising CO₂ emissions are tightly associated with global temperature increases.

Does renewable-energy adoption mitigate this relationship?

Yes, but the effect is partial and heterogeneous across countries. Time-series indices show renewable-energy share remained flat or declined for many years before rising in the late 2010s, suggesting slow global adoption. PCA loadings place renewable energy on an axis opposite to CO₂ emissions, signaling a structural contrast between carbon-intensive and cleaner economies. SHAP and LIME analyses consistently show that higher renewable-energy shares reduce predicted temperature anomalies, confirming a measurable cooling influence. However, this effect is smaller compared to the influence of population and emissions. Thus, renewable energy does mitigate warming pressures, but insufficient global deployment limits its overall impact on the CO₂–temperature link.

Which regions have shown a decoupling of economic growth from emissions?

Clustering and PCA results highlight three broad groups of countries: Cluster 3 (high-GDP, high-population emitters) – large contributors to CO₂ with strong coupling between economic growth and emissions. Cluster 1 (mid-income, moderate emissions) – economies still transitioning and showing partial decoupling. Cluster 2 (high-renewable, low-emissions countries) – these countries demonstrate the clearest decoupling, achieving economic growth with minimal emissions increases due to strong clean-energy penetration. The PCA and clustering therefore reveal that advanced economies with high renewable-energy shares—for example, Northern European nations—have achieved the most successful decoupling, while rapidly industrializing regions continue to scale both GDP and emissions together.

title: 3  3. Exploratory Analysis
text:
3.5 8. Limitations of the Analysis
A key limitation is data availability and consistency. Not all countries report complete annual records for CO₂, temperature anomalies, renewable-energy share, or GDP, leading to missing values and potential sampling bias. Additionally, temperature anomalies represent global or national averages, which may overlook local climate dynamics and variability. Machine learning models like Random Forests capture nonlinearities but cannot infer causal mechanisms, meaning observed relationships reflect correlations rather than definitive causal pathways. Lastly, renewable-energy data do not differentiate between types of renewables or policy contexts, which limits deeper interpretation.

title: 3  3. Exploratory Analysis
text:
3.6 9. Future Work
Future studies could incorporate sector-level emissions, energy-source granularity, and policy intervention data to better understand the mechanisms behind decoupling and energy transitions. Incorporating spatial climate models, carbon-intensity metrics, and time-lag effects could strengthen causal insights. Experimenting with deep learning, gradient boosting, or dynamic panel models may improve forecast accuracy. Expanding the dataset to include land-use change, methane emissions, and climate policy indices would offer a more holistic picture of global warming drivers and mitigation pathways.

title: 4  4. Final Project Conclusion
text: This project shows that global temperature change is closely linked to how countries grow, consume energy, and develop over time. The analysis consistently demonstrated that CO₂ emissions rise alongside temperature anomalies, confirming the strong relationship between human activity and global warming. PCA, clustering, and machine learning added deeper insight by showing that countries fall into distinct patterns: some grow rapidly with high emissions, some still emit little despite rising temperatures, and a few have started to grow economically while keeping emissions low through renewable energy adoption. These findings reinforce that climate change is influenced not only by emissions themselves but also by population size, development patterns, and how quickly countries shift toward cleaner energy. The project also shows that renewable energy plays a meaningful role in reducing warming pressure, even if its impact is still smaller compared to population and economic activity. The Random Forest model and SHAP explanations highlight that higher renewable-energy shares consistently lower predicted temperature anomalies, suggesting that scaling clean energy can make a real difference globally. Overall, the analysis demonstrates that while climate change is a global challenge, countries do not contribute equally or follow the same trajectory. The insights gained underline the importance of investing in renewables, improving energy efficiency, and supporting countries that face warming despite contributing very little to global emissions. This project emphasizes that data-driven understanding is essential for designing fair and effective climate strategies in the real world.
